title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 85–86
description: Advanced abbreviations, acronyms and bibliographic shorthand; productive and evaluative meanings of English prefixes in context.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from the user-supplied book. Vocabulary choices and usage are checked against the specified units, exercises and answer key. Translations, notes and sample sentences are original; source passages and exercises are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 85 and 86 teaching sections A–D and A–C respectively, exercises 85.1–85.4 and 86.1–86.4, and corresponding answer-key entries. Register, pronunciation, prefix meaning and lexical contrasts were reviewed.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is provided only when sufficiently confident. Blank IPA indicates no reliable entry-level transcription was established. Initialisms have short target-focused speechText where necessary; connected speech is not transcribed.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing text is in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared unit teaching texts, tables, exercises and answers; produced original example sentences and checked collocations, register, translation and provenance. JSON structural conformity, uniqueness and static audio targets verified programmatically against the canonical reference.
audit.limitations: No bundled MP3 audio; browser import, speech synthesis and speech recognition were not tested. Abbreviation pronunciation may vary by context or accent, and bibliographic conventions vary with citation style.

units.title: Unit 85 — Abbreviations and acronyms
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 85. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Language and writing · initialisms, acronyms and academic references
learningObjectives: Understand initialisms read letter by letter and distinguish them from pronounceable acronyms.
Recognise common blends and shortened forms, including computing and media vocabulary.
Interpret abbreviated directions, dates and invitation instructions appropriately.
Read bibliographic abbreviations and apply them correctly to academic references.

Facing exercise page and pertinent answer-key entries

items.example: Several renewable sources, e.g. solar and wind power, are included in the report.
items.note: Latin exempli gratia; introduces examples rather than a restatement. Usually read aloud as “for example” in continuous prose.

items.example: The prototype has one remaining fault, i.e. an intermittent power failure.
items.note: Latin id est; clarifies or restates something, rather than listing examples.

items.example: The manuscript is believed to date from around AD 900.
items.note: Anno Domini; calendar designation associated with the Christian era. CE is a widely used alternative.

items.example: The temple was built in the fourth century CE.
items.note: Common Era; a calendar label for the same year numbers as AD, without an explicitly Christian designation.

items.example: The settlement was founded around 300 BC.
items.note: Before Christ; used for years before the common calendar era. BCE is an alternative.

items.example: Archaeologists dated the artefact to about 600 BCE.
items.note: Before the Common Era; corresponds to BC in year numbering.

items.example: The proposal must comply with relevant EU regulations.
items.note: European Union; the two letters are normally said separately.

items.example: Visitors need to show valid ID at reception.
items.note: Identity document or proof of identity; standard in security and administrative contexts.

items.example: NB: The application deadline has been brought forward by a week.
items.note: Latin nota bene; a written instruction to notice an important point. Often found in notes and instructions.

items.example: The researchers warned against treating an IQ score as a complete measure of ability.
items.note: Intelligence quotient; a score from a particular form of cognitive testing.

items.example: The instructions continue on the back of the sheet; PTO.
items.note: Please turn over; typically printed at the foot of a page.

items.example: Save a second copy of the dataset to a USB drive.
items.note: Universal Serial Bus; a connection standard for peripherals and storage devices.

items.example: The FAQ explains how to reset a forgotten password.
items.note: Frequently asked questions; commonly a webpage section. Usually pronounced as individual letters, not a word.

items.pt: o quanto antes; assim que possível
items.example: Please send the revised schedule ASAP so we can inform the team.
items.note: As soon as possible; informal or business shorthand that may sound abrupt in some messages.

items.example: The organisers reserved a separate entrance for VIP guests.
items.note: Very important person; often used attributively, as in VIP lounge.

items.example: The invitation asks all guests to RSVP by Friday.
items.note: From French répondez s’il vous plaît; asks invitees to reply, normally indicating attendance.

items.example: A witness reported a UFO, but its identity was never established.
items.note: Unidentified flying object; a sighting need not be evidence of an alien spacecraft.

items.pt: quitinete de cômodo único; quarto com área de estar
items.example: She rented a small bedsit while completing her postgraduate course.
items.note: British English: a single room serving as both bedroom and living area, typically with limited facilities.

items.pt: comédia de situação; seriado de comédia
items.example: The sitcom follows three colleagues sharing a flat in London.
items.note: Short for situation comedy; a television or radio comedy about recurring characters.

items.example: The festival is screening several classic sci-fi films.
items.note: Informal shortening of science fiction; commonly used for films, literature and TV.

items.example: You can find more info about the scholarship on the website.
items.note: Informal shortening of information; often used in digital communication.

items.pt: dados biográficos; resumo da trajetória pessoal e profissional
items.example: Applicants were asked to provide biodata outlining their qualifications and experience.
items.note: Biographical data; a concise account of someone’s background and achievements.

items.example: The director made a biopic about a pioneering physicist.
items.note: A film about the life of a real person; contracted from biographical picture.

items.example: The conference centre provides free Wi-Fi throughout the building.
items.note: A common name for wireless networking. The textbook associates the term with “wireless fidelity”.

items.example: Medical advances have greatly improved the treatment of AIDS.
items.note: Acquired immune deficiency syndrome; pronounced as a single word, unlike a letter-by-letter initialism.

items.pt: OTAN; Organização do Tratado do Atlântico Norte
items.example: NATO members discussed the joint security exercise.
items.note: North Atlantic Treaty Organisation; normally pronounced as a word.

items.example: Never write your PIN on the back of your bank card.
items.note: Personal identification number; pronounced like the ordinary word pin, not as three letters.

items.example: VAT is included in the advertised price.
items.note: Value-added tax; in British English can be read as “vat” or spelled out as three letters.

items.example: The pressure curve is reproduced in fig. 4 of the report.
items.note: Abbreviation for figure, usually followed by a number in academic or technical documents.

items.example: The reference lists Patel as ed. of the collected volume.
items.note: Bibliographic abbreviation for editor (singular); not necessarily the author of the chapters.

items.example: In the bibliography, Roberts and Ahmed are listed as eds.
items.note: Plural form of ed., meaning editors.

items.example: The definition is given on p. 72 of the handbook.
items.note: Bibliographic shorthand for one page. Contrast pp. for several pages.

items.example: The experiment is described on pp. 14–19 of the manual.
items.note: Bibliographic shorthand for pages; a range includes the pages at both endpoints.

items.example: The findings are discussed in Miller (2018); cf. Santos (2020).
items.note: Latin confer; directs the reader to compare a cited source, not merely to read it.

items.example: The review by Taylor et al. proposes a different explanation.
items.note: Latin et alia; used for a work with multiple authors, commonly three or more, depending on citation style.

units.title: Unit 86 — Prefixes: creating new meanings
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 86. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Word formation · evaluative, positional and productive prefixes
learningObjectives: Infer how common prefixes change a word’s meaning, including negative, repeated and comparative senses.
Distinguish the excess, position and figurative uses of over-, under- and up-.
Use modern electronic and environmental prefixes in context.
Understand the lexical meanings of less frequent con-/com-, pro- and e- formations.

sectionsChecked: Full teaching page including distinctions, definitions and source usage notes
Facing exercise page and pertinent answer-key entries

items.example: A sarcastic remark would be inappropriate in this formal report.
items.note: Negative prefix in- indicates that something is unsuitable for a situation.

items.example: The system is incapable of processing more than one request at a time.
items.note: Pattern: incapable of + noun or -ing form.

items.example: A small measurement inaccuracy affected the final estimate.
items.note: The noun refers to a lack of accuracy; contrast accurate and inaccurate.

items.example: His inability to access the database delayed the analysis.
items.note: Pattern: inability to + infinitive; not interchangeable in every context with incapable of.

items.example: The team had to make a decision using imperfect information.
items.note: The negative prefix changes in- to im- before p in this word.

items.example: The children were warned not to misbehave during the museum visit.
items.note: Mis- can mean badly or wrongly; normally used for conduct.

items.example: Sharing the access code could allow someone to misuse the system.
items.note: Mis- marks an incorrect, improper or harmful use of something.

items.example: Students from overseas now outnumber local students in the programme.
items.note: Transitive verb: A outnumbers B; compares group sizes.

items.pt: ter mais peso ou importância que; superar
items.example: The potential benefits outweigh the short-term costs.
items.note: Usually figurative: the importance of one consideration exceeds another.

items.example: The panel agreed to reconsider its original decision.
items.note: Re- signals considering something again.

items.example: The council intends to redevelop the old industrial site.
items.note: Re- indicates developing a site or project again, often in a new form.

items.example: The unexpected results forced us to rethink our approach.
items.note: Rethink a decision, plan or assumption: reconsider and possibly change it.

items.example: Small retailers increasingly depend on e-commerce to reach distant customers.
items.note: Electronic commerce: the buying and selling of goods or services online.

items.pt: leitor digital de livros; dispositivo de leitura eletrônica
items.example: She carries an e-reader instead of printed textbooks when travelling.
items.note: Electronic device designed primarily for reading digital books.

items.example: The report examines regulations concerning e-cigarettes.
items.note: Electronic cigarette; modern devices vary, so the source’s description is not a universal technical specification.

items.pt: ecologicamente correto; menos prejudicial ao meio ambiente
items.example: The supplier has introduced eco-friendly packaging made from recycled material.
items.note: Eco- suggests environmental concern; the label alone does not prove zero environmental impact.

items.example: The regional plan proposes an eco-city powered mainly by renewable energy.
items.note: A city designed to use resources efficiently and reduce pollution.

items.pt: ativista ambiental; defensor combativo do meio ambiente
items.example: The newspaper described the campaigner as an eco-warrior.
items.note: Informal, potentially approving or dismissive label for an outspoken environmental activist.

items.section: B · Over-: excess, above and across
items.example: In my view, the award-winning restaurant is overrated.
items.note: Over- marks excessive praise compared with actual merit.

items.section: B · Over-: excess, above and across
items.example: Several reviewers considered the hotel overpriced for its facilities.
items.note: Over- describes a price judged too high relative to value.

items.section: B · Over-: excess, above and across
items.example: Two branches overhang the path behind the laboratory.
items.note: Over- indicates something extending above another surface or area.

items.pt: fazer sombra sobre; deixar à sombra
items.section: B · Over-: excess, above and across
items.example: A neighbouring tower overshadows the garden each afternoon.
items.note: Literal meaning: block light by casting a shadow over another place.

items.section: B · Over-: excess, above and across
items.example: Her early achievements were overshadowed by the controversy.
items.note: Figurative meaning: make an event or achievement seem less important or impressive.

items.section: B · Over-: excess, above and across
items.example: The interviewer overstepped the mark by asking about private medical details.
items.note: Idiom meaning cross a social or behavioural boundary; often used for offensive remarks.

items.pt: durante a noite; de um dia para o outro
items.section: B · Over-: excess, above and across
items.example: The laboratory left the instruments running overnight.
items.note: Crosses from one day to the next; can also mean very suddenly in other contexts.

items.section: B · Under-: deficiency, position and negative behaviour
items.example: Do not underestimate the effort required to verify the measurements.
items.note: Under- marks an estimate below the real amount or importance.

items.pt: com pessoal insuficiente; com falta de funcionários
items.section: B · Under-: deficiency, position and negative behaviour
items.example: The clinic was understaffed during the holiday period.
items.note: Too few workers for the necessary work.

items.pt: sob os pés; no chão onde se pisa
items.section: B · Under-: deficiency, position and negative behaviour
items.example: The path was wet and slippery underfoot after the rain.
items.note: Refers to the state of the ground beneath someone’s feet.

items.pt: subjacente; fundamental; que está por trás
items.section: B · Under-: deficiency, position and negative behaviour
items.example: The report addresses the underlying causes of the system failures.
items.note: Underlying problems are deeper or less obvious than the visible symptoms.

items.section: B · Under-: deficiency, position and negative behaviour
items.example: Repeated public criticism began to undermine confidence in the project.
items.note: Figuratively weaken an authority, achievement, argument or relationship.

items.section: B · Under-: deficiency, position and negative behaviour
items.example: The rival firm used underhand tactics to gain an advantage.
items.note: Negative adjective suggesting covert and potentially dishonest methods.

items.example: The airline agreed to upgrade our seats at no extra charge.
items.note: Move something to a higher standard or class; also common for software or hardware.

items.example: There has been an upturn in demand since the new product launched.
items.note: A favourable change, often in economic activity or performance.

items.example: The participants were invited to converse in English after the seminar.
items.note: Relatively formal verb for having a conversation; differs from converse meaning opposite.

items.pt: solidarizar-se com o sofrimento de alguém; lamentar junto
items.example: We commiserated with her after the rejection of her grant application.
items.note: Pattern: commiserate with someone over/about a setback.

items.example: The department sent condolences to the family after their loss.
items.note: Usually plural: offer/send/express condolences to somebody, especially after a death.

items.example: The cooking oil began to congeal as it cooled.
items.note: Become thick or solid, often after cooling; commonly used of liquids or fat.

items.example: Even small amounts of residue can contaminate the sample.
items.note: Make something polluted, unsafe or impure by introducing an unwanted substance.

items.example: The university launched a campaign to promote international research partnerships.
items.note: Can mean encourage or publicise; also means raise someone to a higher position.

items.example: Unverified copies of the document began to proliferate online.
items.note: Increase rapidly in number, often referring to a process with consequences.

items.example: He tends to procrastinate when faced with a difficult writing assignment.
items.note: Delay doing something that needs to be done, often habitually.

items.example: The species must procreate successfully to maintain its population.
items.note: Formal term for producing offspring; applies to humans and animals.

items.example: A security guard had to eject a spectator who was disrupting the event.
items.note: Formal verb meaning force out of a place; also used mechanically for a cartridge or disk.

items.example: The sensor emits a brief signal when the threshold is crossed.
items.note: Formal verb for giving out light, sound, heat, gas or another substance.

items.example: The spokesperson overstated the benefits of the proposed reform.
items.note: Over- expresses excessive emphasis or exaggeration.

items.pt: trem de pouso; parte inferior de um veículo
items.example: The aircraft made an emergency landing after a fault in its undercarriage.
items.note: For aircraft, the assembly that supports the plane when it is on the ground.

items.example: The remaining instructions are printed overleaf.
items.note: Formal written direction: on the other side of the sheet of paper.

items.example: His overbearing manner discouraged colleagues from asking questions.
items.note: Describes a person who tries to control others excessively.

items.example: The research project remained underfunded despite its promising early results.
items.note: Receiving less money than necessary for the work.

items.pt: para fora de uma embarcação; ao mar
items.example: A passenger fell overboard during the storm.
items.note: Movement over the side of a boat or ship into the water.

items.example: Her contribution to the project has been consistently underrated.
items.note: Not appreciated or valued as highly as it deserves; opposite of overrated.

items.example: The manager handed the tedious task to an underling.
items.note: A subordinate, usually a dismissive or derogatory term.
